articles.title: The Dell XPS 13 is the first real competitor to the MacBook Neo
articles.summary: Even the base XPS 13 is an excellent laptop. But you’re still gonna want the 16GB model.
articles.body: Dell’s last XPS 13 was meant to be a farewell before the company sunset the entire XPS brand. But it was a bitter ending, and an overpriced one as well. Earlier this year, Dell resurrected the XPS name with the excellent (and very expensive) XPS 14 and 16. And now, it’s reinvented the XPS 13 as a much more affordable thin-and-light to take on the MacBook Neo. Call it another comeback. The 2026 XPS 13 has the nicest hardware you’ll find in a new $700 laptop outside of Apple’s Neo. The core components — the screen, keyboard, trackpad, and speakers — are all great or excellent. It’s an exquisite package in a sleek and very thin ultra-portable. And unlike other Windows 11 laptops that struggled to get by with 8GB of RAM, the XPS 13 feels competent even with that limited memory allocation. But even though it’s great that there’s an 8GB Windows laptop in 2026 that’s not dead on arrival, you’re still going to want the 16GB version (which I’ve also been testing) for $1,000. And sadly, no configuration of the XPS 13 includes a headphone jack. [Product: Dell XPS 13 (2026) | I’ve been testing two XPS 13 configurations with the same six-core Intel Core 5 320 “Wildcat Lake” processor and 512GB SSD. Their singular difference is memory: The base $799.99 model has 8GB of RAM and the $999.99 one has 16GB. I’ve been working off this pair quite a bit for a couple weeks, and the hardware is brilliant. When I got them, that 8GB / 512GB configuration was the base model and cost $699.99. But in early September, Dell created a new $699.99 base model with just 256GB of storage, and raised the price of the 512GB models by $100 each. Sadly these kinds of pricing shenanigans are commonplace in our ongoing RAMageddon nightmare. --- Component report card * Screen: A * Webcam: A * Keyboard: B * Trackpad: B * Port selection: D * Speakers: B * Number of ugly stickers to remove: 1 --- The XPS 13 is the nicest-looking and -feeling Windows laptop you’re going to find at this price. It’s just as sleek as a MacBook Neo or Air, and at 2.2 pounds / 1kg and 0.5 inches / 12.7mm thick, it’s lighter than the Air and almost as thin. The XPS is an exquisite laptop to hold, and it practically disappears into a bag. The screen has much thinner bezels than a Neo, and it’s equally bright and colorful — but with 120Hz refresh and touch support rather than the Neo’s 60Hz non-touch screen. It even has an anti-glare finish the Neo doesn’t offer. The speakers sound surprisingly good for such a compact laptop, offering a well-rounded sound that gets plenty loud. The mechanical trackpad is small, even shorter than the Neo’s, but its only major downside is that it doesn’t physically click in all four corners. Even the webcam impressed me, rendering very good color and handling poor light or backlighting just fine. And the keyboard? Somebody tell Dell’s designers to put this nice tactile chiclet-style keyboard on everything and give up on that latticeless look on other XPS laptops. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Battery life and thermals aren’t amazing, but they’re adequate. The bottom chassis frequently warms your lap, with its hottest point reaching as high as 104 degrees Fahrenheit / 40 degrees Celsius, but the keyboard deck stays cool. As for the battery, it typically got me seven hours of continuous mixed usage (lots of Chrome tabs, a few video calls, and streaming a few albums with the screen on most of the time) or up to 10 hours during a much lighter meeting-free day. I’d usually prefer a thicker laptop for the sake of more battery, but I’ve been smitten enough by the XPS’s small and light frame to feel this is passable — even though the Neo lasts several hours longer on an even lower-capacity battery. The XPS 13 has two 10Gbps USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 ports, one on either side, and both support charging and video-out. But why, oh why, does this laptop not have a headphone jack? Even if you rarely use 3.5mm audio it’s nice to have as a fallback option. As for raw performance, both versions of the XPS 13 fall well behind the MacBook Neo’s A18 Pro in synthetic benchmark tests like Geekbench, though the 16GB model is significantly closer in our Premiere 4K export test. And the XPS’s six-core Wildcat Lake chip is night-and-day better than the five-core version found in the Chuwi UniBook, which took over an hour to export. The extra performance core and extra GPU core in the XPS 13 make a notable difference, and so does its speedy storage. The XPS 13’s SSD read speed is nearly three times as fast as the Chuwi, and nearly four times as fast as the Neo. In day-to-day use of the XPS 13, 8GB of RAM actually feels passable, unlike with the Chuwi and recent Surface Laptop 13-inch. I have used it without any major failings or crashes, and it’s mostly gotten by okay when all I ask of it is simple web-based stuff. But having only 8GB of memory does occasionally slow you down while multitasking. For example, with a dozen or more Chrome tabs open on it I occasionally had to wait for my tabs to reload when I switched back and forth between them. That’s a normal Chrome feature to save memory, but it happens a lot on the 8GB XPS 13. And when I was bouncing between a couple dozen Chrome tabs and messaging colleagues on Slack — not an unusual workload — even tabs I had used just minutes before got dumped from memory and needed to reload. [Image: I dig that the XPS branding is back. The last XPS 13 just had the boring Dell logo on the lid. I was working late one night, writing up some recent news, and slowly getting frustrated as those split-second delays added up. Switching tabs, swiping between virtual desktops, swiping up into Windows’ Task View — it all worked, but every so often the swipes and quick changes felt a little slower. I then made the mistake of opening Adobe Photoshop to do a few simple image crops, and I suddenly regretted life itself. It was the kind of edit that normally takes me a couple minutes, but every little drop-down menu or drag-and-drop in Photoshop felt excruciatingly slow. These are the ways you still feel the friction of 8GB of RAM on Windows, even in an otherwise brilliant laptop. The 16GB XPS 13 doesn’t have those same pain points — not at this workload, at least. Going up to 16GB of RAM gives you adequate headroom so Windows isn’t constantly trying to reallocate memory, and you can actually do the occasional demanding task like opening and resizing an unexpectedly large image file. The XPS’s speedy SSD seems to help compared to other 8GB laptops I’ve used recently, but you know what helps even more? More RAM. It’s just a shame you’re paying an extra $300 to get it in the 16GB / 512GB XPS 13 config, which now costs $999.99 — it was a $200 upcharge mere weeks ago. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: While the MacBook Neo is still the clear winner in performance, the XPS 13 is its best competition yet. Dell has positioned this as an affordable student laptop, just like the Neo, and the company has mostly nailed it — at least in the US, where the XPS 13 seems to be much cheaper than in other regions (sorry, international friends). The models with 8GB RAM are even the same price as the Neo, at $699.99 for 265GB of storage and $799.99 for 512GB. At the time of this review, Dell still offers a $100 discount for high school and college students, matching Apple’s education discount on the Neo. But the promo is temporary, whereas Apple’s own $100 student discount has no set expiration. You could still save much more with a laptop like the HP OmniBook 3 that I just reviewed, getting you more RAM, more ports, better battery life, slightly more performance (except in graphics), and a much bigger screen for only $500-ish — but it’s a bulkier laptop that doesn’t feel or look remotely as nice as the XPS 13. The MacBook Neo has jump-started new competition in this $700-ish laptop space, all while RAMageddon rages on and makes everything more expensive (including the Neo itself). We’re about to see even more laptop makers launch their answers to the Neo, and hopefully that means more great, affordable choices — for students or just about anyone in need. The XPS 13 is the frontrunner of MacBook Neo competitors for now, and it shows that an 8GB Windows laptop can actually work okay. But you should still get the 16GB model if you can swing it. --- 2026 Dell XPS 13 specs (as reviewed) * Display: 13.4-inch 2560 x 1600 30–120Hz touchscreen LCD, 500 nits, anti-glare * CPU: Intel Series 3 Core 5 320 (6 cores) * GPU: Intel Graphics (2 cores) * RAM: 8GB, 16GB LPDDR5X * Storage: 512GB M.2 NVMe SSD * Webcam: 1080p IR camera * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 * Ports: 2x USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 (10 Gbps) with DisplayPort and Power Delivery (one on each side) * Biometrics: Windows Hello face unlock * Weight: 2.2 pounds / 1kg * Dimensions: 11.69 x 7.9 x 0.5 inches / 296.9 x 200.66 x 12.7mm * Battery: 52Wh * Price (8GB / 256GB): $699.99 * Price (8GB / 512GB): $799.99 * Price (16GB / 512GB): $999.99 --- Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

articles.title: macOS 27 is available now
articles.summary: Apple released macOS 27 Golden Gate on Monday, bringing the new Siri AI assistant, Liquid Glass improvements, improved performance, and more. The update is compatible with all Macs with Apple Silicon, but no Intel Macs.
articles.body: Apple released macOS 27 Golden Gate on Monday, which brings the new Siri AI assistant, Liquid Glass improvements, improved performance, and more. The update is compatible with all Macs with Apple Silicon, but not Intel Macs — Apple released its final big update for Intel-based Macs last year with macOS Tahoe. Siri AI is arguably the biggest feature in macOS 27, and it allows you to ask questions, search through things involving your personal context like photos and emails, and take actions in apps such as Messages and Reminders. There’s a new dedicated Siri app that keeps an archive of your chats for easier reference. However, Siri AI will initially launch as a beta and will only be available in English. As for Liquid Glass, Apple says the update offers “uniform refraction and improved contrast,” and there is a new slider that makes Liquid Glass elements more or less opaque. And there’s one other major UI change worth celebrating: consistent window corner radii.

articles.title: Mikayla Matthews Quits ‘Secret Lives Of Mormon Wives’: “There’s No Amount Of Money Worth Going Against My Morals”
articles.summary: Mikayla Matthews is leaving The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives amid turmoil in MomTok. The influencer and Hulu star shared the news in a social media post as t...
articles.body:
Mikayla Matthews is leaving The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives amid turmoil in MomTok.

The influencer and Hulu star shared the news in a social media post as the cast was recently seen in Italy filming Season 6 of the reality series.

"I made my decision over a week ago, after hearing some news, that I will not be continuing the show at this moment," Matthews posted on Instagram. "I've said from the beginning of this that I'm not comfortable being a part of something that continues to platform behavior I don't agree especially given my own experience growing up in a home with multiple forms of abuse."

She continued, "There's no amount of money worth going against my morals or changing the stance I've had since I first saw and heard the things that made me feel this strongly. And for me personally, continuing to directly profit from this behavior feels wrong and unethical. It feels like a disservice to the children, everyone's healing and the millions of people watching."

Matthews is seemingly referring to her co-star Taylor Frankie Paul, whose personal life has been at the center of drama on Secret Lives of Mormon Wives since the first season. Production for Season 5 of the series was paused after domestic violence allegations from Paul's ex, Dakota Mortensen, with whom she shares a child. Legal actions, a custody battle, and an old resurfaced video showing Paul physically assaulting Mortensen were released ahead of the release of The Bachelorette , which prompted ABC to cancel its premiere.

On the most recent season of SLOMW , Matthews and Paul clashed over the latter not wanting any criticism of her life. Although Matthews and Paul mended things on camera, things off-camera didn't seem to be good.

Matthews points out that the children ultimately suffer from continuing to expose their troubling lives on camera. Hulu will seemingly continue to work with Paul, which Matthews doesn't think is good for her mental health or for the rest of the cast and their children.

"This show has been a huge part of my life and has helped me provide for my family," Matthews continued. "I'm so grateful for the experience, and will continue sharing my story, my health and advocating for myself and others this shouldn't be 'relatable' or entertainment in anyway. Supporting an ADULT doesn't mean constantly making excuses for toxic behavior while giving unconditional sympathy and grace with zero accountability or change. I was in that enabling cycle for years, and I'm not going to be a part of that again! love you all."

articles.title: Today’s Vergecast: Who is the $1,059 Steam VR headset for?
articles.summary:
Sean Hollister got his hands and face on Valve’s new VR headset, the Steam Frame. It’s expensive, starting at more than $1,000. It’s buggy — he and CNET’s Scott Stein both felt like beta testers as they reviewed it. But it’s also full of interesting ideas, including the promise that Steam games could one day come to your mobile phone. This week on The Vergecast, Sean and Scott discuss who exactly this device is for, in a world that mostly seems to have moved on from VR.

articles.title: Apple Home’s new security camera features cost up to $60 a month
articles.summary: Apple Intelligence upgrades to HomeKit Secure Video come with a steep cost.
articles.body: With the public release of iOS 27 and tvOS 27, Apple Home is getting an injection of Apple Intelligence — but you’ll have to pay more for it. Apple Intelligence for Home brings AI-powered video summaries to HomeKit Secure Video, so you can get short text descriptions of who and what compatible security cameras saw, along with the clip. It also adds a new video search feature and the ability to stitch footage from multiple cameras into one clip, making it easier to keep an eye on what’s happening around your home without scrolling through footage. [Image: AI-generated video summaries provide text descriptions of what a camera sees. But to get these features, you’ll need to pay $9.99 a month for the 2TB iCloud Plus plan (or $39.95 a month for an Apple One Premier subscription) — and that’s just for one camera. According to an Apple support page, to add Apple Intelligence to a second camera, you’ll have to pay $29.99 a month for the 6TB plan. For up to five cameras, it’s a whopping $59.99 a month for the 12TB plan. No word on whether you can add more than five cameras. (Recordings from HomeKit-connected cameras don’t count toward your storage quota.) That’s way too expensive. While the improved video features are useful — I’ve been testing them in beta and have been impressed — they’re not good enough to justify that big a price jump. HomeKit Secure Video has always been behind a paywall, but it started at a very reasonable $1 a month. That’s for the 50GB iCloud Plus plan, which includes recorded footage from one camera, plus smart alerts and facial recognition. For more cameras, you bump up to 2TB / $9.99 a month (up to five), and 6TB / $29.99 a month or higher for unlimited cameras. But the cost for the Apple Intelligence features is a huge increase. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: I currently pay $40 a month for Apple One Premier, which includes 2TB of iCloud storage and gets me HomeKit Secure Video support for five cameras. With the new pricing tier, I keep those benefits and now get Apple Intelligence on one camera. But to get it on all five cameras, I’d need to pay an additional $60 a month. That’s $720 a year, for a total of $1,200. Amazon’s Ring and Google Nest charge around $20 a month for subscription tiers that include similar AI-powered features for their cameras, and both companies offer more features than Apple currently does. An iCloud Plus plan does include storage for photos, files, and device backups, and higher plans may get you higher limits for Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features, but Apple hasn’t released any details about that. The good news is that none of this changes what you get with HomeKit Secure Video today, and the new software releases have added under-the-hood upgrades that improve speed and reliability, plus the service now supports 4K video resolution. But while Apple Intelligence feels like a significant improvement for Apple Home, at these prices, the value just isn’t there. Screenshots by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: Roborock finally brings a roller mop to its flagship robovac.
articles.summary:
The company’s Saros 20 Flow goes on sale today for $1,499.99 (down from $1,699.99). At 3.53 inches tall, it’s one of the slimmest roller mop models, and with 36,000 Pa suction, camera-based obstacle recognition, and the ability to climb multi-layer thresholds, this robot should be able to get the job done. I got a first look at IFA last week and plan to test it soon.
